title: 50 KPIs for Business Success: Formulas and Examples from Finance to Product Development
desc: Fifty KPIs across nine functions, each with a formula and worked example, plus the types of KPIs and how to cascade them to each team member.
body:
A key performance indicator (KPI) is a measure that shows whether you are making progress toward a specific business goal. This list of 50 was first published in 2023. It has been revised: formulas are now given for every KPI, several worked examples have been corrected (return on investment was calculated on revenue instead of gain, and Net Promoter Score was described as a percentage of customers), and duplicates have been removed. Two shorter articles on types of KPIs and on KPIs for individual team members have also been folded into this one.

Types of KPIs

Most KPI types come in pairs. The useful habit is to pair a lagging KPI, which tells you whether you got there, with one or two leading KPIs, which tell you early enough to act.

TypeWhat it meansExample
LeadingPredicts a result before it happensLate purchase orders this week
LaggingReports a result after it happenedOn-time delivery last month
InputResources put inTraining hours
ProcessHow well the work runsChangeover time
OutputWhat the work producedGood units per hour
OutcomeThe effect on the customer or the businessCustomer retention
Quantitative and qualitativeA count or ratio, or a rating from feedbackScrap rate; customer comments coded by theme
Financial and non-financialMeasured in money, or in time, quality or peopleGross margin; first pass yield

Finance and accounting

KPIWhat it showsFormulaExample
Revenue growth rateHow fast sales are growing(Revenue this period − revenue last period) ÷ revenue last period$1.5M vs $1.2M last year: 25%
Gross profit marginWhat is left after the direct cost of what you sold(Revenue − cost of goods sold) ÷ revenue$1.5M revenue, $1.05M COGS: 30%
Return on investment (ROI)Whether a project earned more than it cost(Gain from the investment − cost) ÷ cost$100,000 spent, $150,000 extra gross profit: 50%
Days sales outstanding (DSO)How long customers take to payAccounts receivable ÷ credit sales × days in the period$100,000 owed, $240,000 credit sales in 90 days: 37.5 days
Debt-to-equity ratioHow much the business relies on borrowingTotal debt ÷ shareholders' equity$500,000 debt, $1M equity: 0.5

People (HR)

KPIWhat it showsFormulaExample
Employee turnover rateHow many people leaveLeavers in the year ÷ average headcount8 leavers, 80 average headcount: 10%
Employee engagementHow committed people are, from a regular surveyShare of respondents who are engaged on a consistent survey56 of 80 engaged: 70%
Time to hireHow long a vacancy stays openDays from approval to accepted offer, averaged30 days
Training hours per employeeInvestment in skillsTotal training hours ÷ headcount1,600 hours, 80 people: 20 hours
Absenteeism rateUnplanned absenceDays absent ÷ scheduled working days320 of 18,400 days: 1.7%

Production and manufacturing

KPIWhat it showsFormulaExample
Overall equipment effectiveness (OEE)How much of planned time makes good product at full speedAvailability × performance × quality90% × 80% × 95% = 68.4%
First pass yieldProduct right first time, without reworkGood units first time ÷ units started900 of 1,000: 90%
Scrap rateMaterial wastedScrapped material ÷ material used100 lb of 1,000 lb: 10%
Unplanned downtimeTime lost to breakdowns and shortagesHours stopped that were not planned6 hours in a 120-hour week: 5%
ThroughputOutput rateGood units ÷ operating time100 units per hour
Manufacturing cycle timeTime from start to finish of one orderFinish date − start date, averaged4 days
Changeover timeTime lost switching productsLast good part of A to first good part of B45 minutes
Capacity utilizationHow much of available capacity is usedActual output ÷ capacity800 of 1,000 units: 80%
Work in progress (WIP)Unfinished work tied up on the floorValue or count of started, unfinished orders$85,000, or 12 orders
Production cost per unitWhat one unit costs to makeTotal production cost ÷ good units$10,000 ÷ 1,000 = $10

Inventory

KPIWhat it showsFormulaExample
Inventory turnoverHow many times stock is used and replacedCost of goods sold ÷ average inventory at cost$1.2M ÷ $200,000 = 6 turns
Days inventory outstanding (DIO)How long stock sits before it is soldAverage inventory ÷ COGS × 365$200,000 ÷ $1.2M × 365 = 61 days
Stock-out rateHow often an item is not available when neededOrder lines short ÷ order lines30 of 1,000 lines: 3%
Carrying costThe yearly cost of holding stockHolding costs ÷ average inventory value$50,000 ÷ $200,000 = 25%
Obsolete inventoryStock you can no longer sellValue of items with no use in 12 months ÷ total inventory value$10,000 ÷ $200,000 = 5%

Warehouse

KPIWhat it showsFormulaExample
Pick accuracyOrders picked correctlyCorrect order lines ÷ lines picked980 of 1,000: 98%
Inventory record accuracyWhether the system matches the shelfItems counted that match the record ÷ items counted198 of 200: 99%
Dock-to-stock timeTime to put received goods awayTime from receipt to available in the system4 hours
Order cycle timeTime to fulfil an orderShip time − order received time1.5 days
Storage utilizationHow full the warehouse isLocations or cubic space used ÷ available750 of 1,000 pallet spaces: 75%

Shipping

KPIWhat it showsFormulaExample
On-time deliveryOrders arriving by the promised dateOrders on time ÷ orders delivered92 of 100: 92%
Order lead timeTime from order to deliveryDelivery date − order date5 days
Order accuracyOrders delivered correct and completeCorrect orders ÷ orders delivered97 of 100: 97%
Freight cost per orderShipping costFreight cost ÷ orders shipped$10,000 ÷ 1,000 = $10
Damage rateGoods damaged in transitOrders with damage claims ÷ orders shipped5 of 1,000: 0.5%

Supply chain and purchasing

KPIWhat it showsFormulaExample
Perfect order rateOrders on time, complete, undamaged and correctly invoicedPerfect orders ÷ total orders85 of 100: 85%
Cash-to-cash cycle timeHow long cash is tied upDIO + DSO − days payable outstanding61 + 37.5 − 45 = 53.5 days
Supplier on-time deliverySupplier reliabilityPurchase order lines received on time ÷ lines received180 of 200: 90%
Supplier defect rateQuality of what you buyDefective units received ÷ units received5 of 1,000: 0.5%
Purchase price variancePaying more or less than planned(Actual price − standard price) × quantity($10.40 − $10.00) × 5,000 = $2,000 unfavourable

Customer service

KPIWhat it showsFormulaExample
Net Promoter Score (NPS)Loyalty: would customers recommend you% promoters (9–10) − % detractors (0–6)60% − 15% = 45
Customer satisfaction (CSAT)Satisfaction with a recent interactionSatisfied responses (4–5 of 5) ÷ responses180 of 200: 90%
Customer retention rateCustomers who stay(Customers at end − new customers) ÷ customers at start(110 − 20) ÷ 100 = 90%
First contact resolutionIssues solved without a follow-upResolved on first contact ÷ total contacts70 of 100: 70%
Average response timeHow long customers wait for a first replyTotal time to first reply ÷ tickets3 working hours

Product development

KPIWhat it showsFormulaExample
Time to marketSpeed from idea to launchLaunch date − project approval date6 months
Projects on scheduleDelivery against planProjects hitting the planned gate date ÷ projects7 of 10: 70%
Development cost vs budgetSpending controlActual cost ÷ budget$540,000 ÷ $500,000 = 108%
New product revenue shareHow much revenue comes from recent productsRevenue from products launched in the last 3 years ÷ total revenue$300,000 ÷ $1.5M = 20%
Early warranty claimsQuality of new products in the fieldUnits with a claim in the first 12 months ÷ units sold12 of 1,000: 1.2%

Examples are illustrative. Benchmarks vary widely by industry and size, so compare yourself with your own trend first.

KPIs for each team member

A company KPI only moves when the people who do the work can see how their part affects it. Cascade each company goal into the department KPIs that drive it, and then into one or two measures each person controls day to day.

Three rules keep individual KPIs fair and useful. Measure what the person controls, not results that depend on other teams. Keep it to two or three measures, so people know what matters. And use them for coaching and problem-solving first; tying pay to a single number invites people to game it.

How to pick your KPIs

  1. Start from three to five business goals, not from this list.
  2. For each goal, choose one lagging and one or two leading KPIs.
  3. Write a one-line definition with the formula, data source, owner and review frequency, so the number means the same thing every month.
  4. Show the trend, not just this month's figure, on a simple dashboard.
  5. Drop any KPI nobody has acted on in six months.
